summary: Defines a Sieve extension for comparing the parts of an address that uses subaddressing, such as ken+sieve@example.org, namely the user and detail parts. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 5233.

plainLanguage.summary: Some mail systems let you add a tag after a plus sign in your address. This memo lets mail filter rules look at the name and the tag separately.

questions: filter email by plus address detail
how to use detail tags in sieve
subtitle: Filter email by examining the user and detail parts of plus-addressed mailboxes.

tldr.problem: Some mail systems allow subaddressing (e.g., ken+sieve@example.org), but Sieve mail filtering rules could not examine the detail part separately from the user part.
tldr.mechanism: This extension adds two address parts, :user and :detail, to Sieve filter rules. The user part is everything before the separator character (typically +), and the detail part is everything after it.
tldr.outcome: Mail filters can now sort messages based on the detail tag in the recipient address, enabling better organization and filtering. The extension was superseded by RFC 5233.

today: RFC 3598 has been superseded by RFC 5233, which provides the same Sieve subaddress extension functionality with refinements.

sections.title: Subaddressing and Mail Filtering
sections.content:
Subaddressing is the practice of appending detail information to the local-part of an email address using a separator character, typically the plus sign (+). This splits the local-part into two sub-parts: the user (original local-part) and the detail (the appended information). For example, in ken+sieve@example.org, 'ken' is the user part and 'sieve' is the detail part. The detail information indicates which mailbox or filter to apply to the message.

The Sieve mail filtering language lets users write rules to automatically process incoming mail. Without this extension, Sieve could not examine the user and detail parts separately; it only saw the full local-part of the address. This extension adds that capability.
sections.plainLanguage: Subaddressing is like adding a note to your mailbox number: ken+sieve means 'for sieve matters'. The extension lets mail filters read that note so they can sort messages better.

sections.title: The Subaddress Extension
sections.content:
The extension defines two new address parts that Sieve commands can use: :user and :detail. The :user argument specifies the part of the local-part that lies to the left of the separator character. If no separator character exists, :user is the entire local-part. The :detail argument specifies the part to the right of the separator. If there is no separator, the detail test evaluates to false. If nothing lies to the right of the separator (e.g., ken+@example.org), the detail is the null key.

Implementations must ensure that the separator character matches what the mail system uses. The extension recommends that implementations allow the separator character to be configurable to work with different mail systems.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension adds two new tags: :user picks the part before the plus sign, and :detail picks the part after it. If you use neither, filters see the whole address as before.

sections.title: Using the Extension in Filter Rules
sections.content:
The :user and :detail address parts work like the existing address parts in Sieve (such as :localpart and :domain). They can be used with Sieve commands that operate on addresses, such as address tests and envelope tests. The RFC gives three example filter rules: one that files messages sent to a mailing-list detail tag into a specific folder, one that discards messages not addressed to the user at the user's domain (ignoring the detail part), and one that redirects messages sent to a particular detail tag to another address.

The envelope address is preferred for subaddress examination because it reflects how the message was actually addressed to reach the recipient, whereas the header address may not contain the detail information if the message passed through mailing lists or aliases.
sections.plainLanguage: You can write rules like: 'If this came to ken+work, put it in the work folder.' The envelope address (where the mail system addressed it) is usually the right place to check, because headers might be changed by mailing lists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC notes that security considerations are those discussed in the base Sieve specification. This extension does not introduce additional security concerns beyond what already exist in mail filtering. As with any mail filtering, care should be taken when writing rules that discard or redirect messages based on address parts, since a missing or malformed detail tag could cause unintended behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: There are no special security issues with this extension beyond the normal concerns in mail filtering: make sure your rules are correct so you do not accidentally delete or misdirect mail.
